variants.name: Guarded trust with routine social life
variants.text: These respondents hold low interpersonal trust and low trust in institutions, yet report a generally routine, middling-satisfied outlook. Their social lives are modest and infrequent, with friends outside the neighborhood seen rarely and relatives seen a few times a month. Financial worry sits alongside an average self-assessed income and a self-placement in the working or middle class. Views on technology and AI lean toward caution and discomfort, while support for science funding is tilted toward spending too little.

variants.name: Mixed-satisfaction middle-income households
variants.text: Here the pattern is one of ambivalent contentment: people describe themselves as pretty happy while being dissatisfied with democracy and with the economy. Financial trajectories are split, some improving and others worsening, but income is usually perceived as average. Taxes feel too high, and social evenings are spread out, with relatives seen more often than non-neighbors. Attitudes toward automation are wary yet not alarmed, and skepticism about how family life suffers from men's work intersects with moderate agreement on technology's benefits.

variants.name: Disengaged, cautious, low-stimulation lives
variants.text: This cluster is characterized by low political interest and a sense that daily life is routine rather than exciting. Respondents rarely spend social evenings outside the neighborhood and often see relatives infrequently, and several had to cut back on work for family reasons. They verify political information only occasionally, express little trust in people or institutions, and feel the economy is poor. Their responses on AI and robots tend toward being uncomfortable with machines doing human tasks, while they also think public science spending is inadequate.

variant_stats.name: Guarded trust with routine social life

variants.name: Trusting, upbeat, financially secure
variants.text: Respondents describe themselves as trusting of others and happy with life, feeling their family finances are stable and above average, while seeing themselves in the upper social tier. They are strongly satisfied with how democracy works, yet they still judge the economy harshly and feel taxes are too high.

variants.name: Pessimistic about economy and technology
variants.text: Respondents are optimistic about personal life and family matters but deeply negative about the national economy and strongly skeptical of technology. Their answers pair strong worry about automation and AI with reluctance to delegate tasks to machines, showing a split between personal contentment and broad societal anxiety.

variants.name: Family-centered, exciting life, institution-minded
variants.text: Respondents place family at the center, often spending evenings with relatives while seldom socializing with outside friends, and they report that family duties have shaped their work choices. They find life exciting and rate most public institutions as fairly trustworthy, while holding traditional views about gendered work-family tradeoffs.

variants.name: Content with system and finances
variants.text: These respondents are generally satisfied with how democracy works and with their own financial situation, which they see as improving over recent years. They view the national economy favorably and feel personally happy, though they regard their life as fairly routine rather than exciting. They tend to see their income as well below average yet place themselves at the top of the social ladder, and they want less federal tax.

variants.name: Engaged but socially withdrawn
variants.text: These respondents follow politics closely and feel strongly about public affairs, while rarely socializing with friends outside their neighborhood or with extended relatives. Their work responsibilities have led them to scale back on commitments to family, and they hold a neutral view on whether men's work crowds out family life. Their interest in civic matters coexists with a quiet, home-centered or solitary daily life.

variants.name: Contented outlook with public-minded priorities
variants.text: These respondents combine a positive personal outlook, feeling happy and seeing their finances as improving, with support for greater public investment, especially in scientific research. They are satisfied with the political system and rate the economy highly, yet still regard their own tax burden as excessive. Their routine-oriented, low-social-activity lifestyle sits alongside confident, upbeat views about the country's direction.

variants.name: Distrustful, dissatisfied, financially squeezed
variants.text: Respondents combine low trust in others and in institutions with deep dissatisfaction about democracy, the economy and their own finances. Their sense of falling behind economically runs alongside a feeling that the system is not working for them, and they see themselves near the bottom of the social ladder. Political engagement is minimal, and they lean toward feeling that taxes are too high.

variants.name: Flat, routine, low-engagement life
variants.text: These people describe their lives as routine or dull and their happiness as only moderate or low. Social contact is sparse, with infrequent evenings with relatives and occasional outings with friends. They are largely indifferent to politics and to technology debates, and tend to hold neutral or middling views on questions about work, family and tech, without strong opinions in either direction.

variants.name: Cautious, middling, mixed-attitude profile
variants.text: Answers cluster around the middle of scales on trust, technology and comfort with AI, rather than at the extremes. Some items point toward caution or worry while others are neutral or accepting, so the overall profile is ambivalent. Economic views are mostly negative, yet attitudes toward science spending and robots are measured, producing a pattern of hedged, undecided responses.

variants.name: Trusting, routine-living family-oriented
variants.text: Respondents lean toward trusting others, see their social life as routine and centered on relatives rather than friends, and spend regular evenings with family. Their trust in others pairs with a steady, uneventful outlook on life, and they feel their family's finances have held steady while sitting well below average. Politically they are engaged but dissatisfied with how democracy works, and they check political information against other sources.

variants.name: Stable but dissatisfied with institutions
variants.text: These answers combine contentment with ordinary life and a middle-of-the-road view of the economy with sharp dissatisfaction toward public systems. Respondents feel moderately happy and see neither good nor bad economic times, yet they are largely unhappy with democratic processes and hold mixed, middling trust in institutions. Their attitudes toward technology are favorable, with clear support for more public science funding, while they remain wary of AI taking on human tasks.

variants.name: Cautious tech skeptics with low finances
variants.text: Respondents tend to report modest finances that have not changed, see themselves in the lower social class, and feel only routine interest in an otherwise unexciting life. They express comfort with technology in daily work and family settings while remaining uneasy about machines and AI performing human actions. They also hold a traditional view of gender and work, and they regard current tax levels as acceptable.
